newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends up in U.S., buoyed by stg, yen weakness.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends up in U.S., buoyed by stg, yen weakness.

text.p: The dollar rose for a second session on Thursday, buoyed by Japanese officials' vocal support of their central bank's low interest rate policy and a potential shake-up at Britain's central bank, dealers said.

"The two biggest factors in trade today have been the selling of yen overnight and the selling of sterling in New York," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice-president at Bank Julius Baer and Co in New York.
The dollar rose to 116.10/15 yen from 115.85/95 at Thursday's open and the British pound fell to $1.6237/42 from $1.6380/90.
Dealers said volatility had decreased from the wide trading ranges seen earlier this week, but nerves remained raw.

"Today trade has been pretty whippy, but at least within a tighter range. There's a lot of nervousness and there's nobody left but the day traders," said John Barlow, senior dealer at Bayerische Landesbank Girozentrale in New York.
Speculation that Bank of England Governor Eddie George might not be reappointed at the end of his five-year term next year sparked a slide in sterling against both the dollar and German mark.
George, nicknamed "Steady Eddie" for his hawkish anti-inflation views, is credited by many with piloting Britain to its best inflation performance for more than 30 years.

Following days of speculation that Japan was prepared to raise interest rates in the near future, the dollar rallied after Japan's Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka told a parliamentary committee meeting that he favored the Bank of Japan's current low interest rate policy.
Comments from Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa, that recent concern over an excessively weak yen had completely disappeared, also boosted the dollar.

And news that the Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd's London branch had made a 10 billion yen ($86.9 million) loss from derivatives played on worries over Japan's already troubled banking sector and further weakened the yen.
The U.S. unit also racked up gains against the Swiss franc despite news Switzerland's central bank elected not to cut official interest rates as had been speculated.
That helped support the dollar against the mark, which closed only slightly higher at 1.6940/50 marks from 1.6930/35. The dollar ended at 1.4145/55 Swiss francs from 1.4108/18.
However, the dollar struggled earlier after new data generated optimism over Germany's economic outlook and the Bundesbank dampened speculation of monetary easing there.
The Ifo business climate index for April jumped to 94.7 from 92.6 -- which took the sting out of a lower than expected 6.7 percent expansion in April German M3 money supply.
Also, Bundesbank council member Olaf Sievert said there was no current leeway for further rate cuts, though he added that there was no reason to consider higher rates in the near future.
The dollar received little boost from the release of the minutes from the March 25 meeting of Federal Reserve policymakers, which resulted in a 25 basis point hike in the federal funds rate target.

"The dollar is still holding firm. I don't think the minutes gave any surprises and no one jumped (to trade) on it," said Stephen Flanagan, senior foreign exchange dealer at Credit Agricole in New York.
The minutes showed Fed officials voted unanimously to raise the fed funds rate 25 basis points, though a few members would have preferred a bigger increase.
In other trading, the dollar rose to Canadian $1.3730/35 from C$1.3708/13. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7770/75 from $0.7821/26.
((-- Roanne Daniels, 212-859-1677))
